planting.note: Plant the bulb with its neck just at the soil surface in autumn so roots and the flattened leaf pair develop through the cool rainy season, then withhold water completely once foliage yellows in late spring.

directions: This Namaqualand bulb produces just two broad, rounded leaves that lie flat against the ground, sometimes with a blistered or shiny textured surface. A low cluster of brush-like cream to greenish flowers with long stamens opens at ground level between the leaves in winter, releasing a sticky nectar that is lapped up by gerbils and other small rodents, which act as pollinators. Grow in a gritty, fast-draining mix in a container or raised bed and keep bone dry through its summer dormancy, since rot from summer moisture is the most common cause of failure outside its native winter-rainfall climate. Give full sun and bring under cover wherever winters are wet and freezing rather than cool and dry.

planting.note: Set the bulb shallowly in a gritty mix in early autumn to start the paired leaves ahead of winter rains, then let the bulb dry out fully once it goes dormant in late spring.

directions: A paired-leaf Cape bulb closely related to M. depressa, with distinctly raised, pustule-like bumps across the shiny green leaf surface that give the species its name. The fragrant, creamy white to pink brush-flowers sit low between the leaves and hold visible blue-tinted nectar in their cupped bases, a feature that helps draw in rodent pollinators at night. Keep it in a well-drained pot of sandy, lean soil, watering through the winter growing season and stopping entirely as the leaves die back in spring. Full sun and a dry summer rest are essential; in climates with summer rain it needs a covered or greenhouse spot to stay dormant correctly.

planting.note: Plant the corm in autumn so sword-shaped leaves emerge with the winter rains, leading to a late-winter to spring bloom, then keep the corm completely dry during its summer dormancy.

directions: A relative of Ferraria crispa, this iris-family corm sends up narrow pleated leaves and star-shaped flowers mottled in muted brown, green, and purplish tones with crisped, wavy-edged petals. Flowers open for only part of the day and give off a faintly putrid, carrion-like odor that lures flies in to carry out pollination. It needs the same sharply drained, gritty soil and bright exposure as other winter-growing Cape corms, and should be kept dry once the foliage dies back for the summer. Because individual flowers are short-lived, plant several corms together so blooms overlap through the season.

planting.note: Leave most of the large bulb exposed above the soil line when planting in autumn, since this species naturally grows with the bulb's upper half sitting in the open air.

directions: Native to the arid Namaqualand and southern Namibian coastal belt, this smaller relative of Boophone disticha forms a large, mostly above-ground bulb with gray-green strap leaves that appear after the flowers. A rounded umbel of narrow pink flowers opens on a bare stalk ahead of the leaves, typically in late summer to autumn as the winter rains approach. All parts of the plant contain toxic alkaloids and should be kept away from pets and children. Grow in extremely sharp-draining mineral soil in full sun and withhold water almost entirely during its summer rest, since it is adapted to some of the driest habitats among Cape bulbs.
sources: Silverhill Seeds — Growing Hints: Bulbous Plants

planting.note: Plant the large bulb with its neck at or just below the soil surface in early autumn; strap-like leaves follow the flower stalk and grow through winter before dying back for a dry summer dormancy.

directions: This large Amaryllis-relative bulb is famous for synchronized mass flowering across the Namaqualand and Western Karoo landscape after good autumn rains, when a leafless stalk pushes up a huge rounded umbel of dozens of pale to deep pink flowers. Strap-shaped leaves emerge only after flowering and persist through the winter growing season before dying back completely as the bulb goes dormant for summer. It is slow to reach flowering size from seed and needs a deep pot or bed of very free-draining soil to accommodate its large bulb. Keep it completely dry and in full sun during summer dormancy, since excess moisture at that time causes bulb rot.

planting.note: Plant bulbs shallowly in autumn in a free-draining mix; this species naturally grows in seasonally damp ground so keep it evenly moist through winter bloom before drying off for summer.

directions: Narrow, grass-like leaves and slender fleshy stems carry clusters of fragrant, brush-shaped white flowers tipped with maroon to red markings, which gave the species its name as though the white blooms were stained or contaminated. It occurs in naturally damper winter-wet sites in the southwestern Cape, so unlike many drier-growing Lachenalia it tolerates more consistent moisture during its winter and spring growing season. Grow it in a pot or bed with good drainage but regular winter water, then let it dry out fully once the foliage dies back in late spring for its summer dormancy. Full sun and a cool, frost-free winter give the best flowering.

planting.note: Plant bulbs shallowly in a gritty mix in autumn to start winter growth, then stop watering completely once leaves yellow in spring to allow a dry summer dormancy.

directions: A small winter-growing Cape bulb named for the raised, bump-like pustules that texture its broad green leaves. Tubular, two-toned flowers in shades of lavender, magenta, pink, or yellow are held above the foliage in winter and early spring and often carry a noticeable fragrance. Like the rest of the genus, it requires a sharply drained, sandy soil mix and completely dry conditions through its summer dormancy to avoid bulb rot. Grow it in full sun in a container where summers are wet, or in a bulb frame or unheated greenhouse in colder climates.

planting.note: Plant corms in autumn, barely covered in a fast-draining mix, so the pleated, hairy leaves and flower spikes develop over the cool wet season ahead of a dry summer dormancy.

directions: Like other Babiana species, this corm produces pleated, softly hairy iris-like leaves, a texture thought to have inspired the Afrikaans name referring to baboons rooting for the corms. It bears intensely fragrant blue flowers marked with white nectar guides on the lower petals, growing naturally in dry fynbos and renosterveld habitats of the winter-rainfall Cape. Grow in full sun in sandy, sharply drained soil, watering through autumn and winter growth and withholding water entirely once the foliage dies down in late spring. It is best grown in a container or raised bed outside Mediterranean climates so the corms can be kept bone dry over summer.

planting.note: Plant corms shallowly in autumn in a lean, fast-draining mix so growth tracks the natural winter rains, then keep completely dry through summer dormancy.

directions: This uncommon Babiana is restricted in the wild to rocky, clay-rich outcrops on the Bokkeveld Plateau near Nieuwoudtville, flowering from winter into early spring. Its pleated, hairy leaves support deep blue-purple, trumpet-shaped flowers with curved tubes and white arrow-shaped markings outlined in darker blue on the lower petals. Because it comes from heavier clay-over-rock sites rather than pure sand, a slightly richer but still sharply drained mix suits it well, with water given through the winter growing months only. Keep it fully dry and in full sun once it goes dormant for summer, and treat it as a collector's bulb for pots or a bulb frame given its restricted native range.
